scenes.narration: Welcome back. Mesh and nodal analysis work well by hand for small circuits. But real networks, like a power grid or a chip, have thousands of branches. To let a computer write all the equations automatically, we need a precise way to describe only how things are connected, ignoring what each element is. That is network topology, using graphs, trees, tie sets and cut sets. Let's build it step by step on a circuit we already know.
scenes.title: NETWORK TOPOLOGY
scenes.subtitle: Graphs, trees, tie-sets and cut-sets

scenes.narration: Here is our example circuit from the language of circuits part: a battery and four resistors, with four nodes, A, B, C and D. To make its graph, we replace every element by a simple line, called a branch, and keep every node as a dot. We number the branches: one is the battery, two is R1, three is R2, four is R3, and five is R4. The graph keeps only the connections. It has four nodes and five branches.

A few more words. A graph is connected if you can reach every node from every other node along branches. It is planar if it can be drawn flat without branches crossing. If we give each branch an arrow showing its current direction, it becomes an oriented, or directed, graph. A subgraph is any part of the graph. And a path is a route from one node to another that never visits a node twice.
scenes.title: Graph vocabulary

scenes.narration: A tree is a part of the graph that connects all the nodes but contains no closed loop. Watch the green branches: one, three and five. They touch all four nodes, and there is no loop among them. That is a tree. Its branches are called twigs. The remaining branches, two and four, shown dashed, are called links. A tree always has n minus one twigs, here three, and the number of links is b minus n plus one, here two, exactly the number of meshes we found earlier.

These counts are the key to everything. Twigs equal n minus one. Links equal b minus n plus one. For our graph, three twigs and two links. Notice: the number of links is the number of independent loop equations, KVL, we need. The number of twigs is the number of independent node equations, KCL, we need. Together they give exactly enough equations to find all five branch currents.

Now add one link back to the tree. It creates exactly one closed loop, called a fundamental loop, or tie set. Watch: adding link R1 makes the loop R1, R2 and the battery. Adding link R3 makes the loop R3, R4 and R2. Each link gives one tie set, so we get two. Writing KVL around each tie set gives the independent loop equations, collected in a tie set matrix. This is mesh analysis written in a form a computer can use.

Now the partner idea. Remove one twig from the tree, and the tree falls into two parts. The set of branches that connect those two parts is called a fundamental cut set. Watch the dashed circle: cutting twig V separates node A, and the cut set is V and R1. Cutting twig R2 separates node B: R2, R1 and R3. Cutting twig R4 separates node C: R4 and R3. Writing KCL for each cut set, total current crossing the cut equals zero, gives the independent node equations, collected in a cut set matrix.

A computer stores the graph as a table called the incidence matrix. Each row is a node, each column a branch. Put plus one if the branch leaves that node, minus one if it enters, and zero otherwise. Dropping the reference node D gives the reduced incidence matrix shown here, for branch directions A to D, A to B, B to D, B to C and C to D. Multiply it by the column of branch currents and set it to zero, and you have KCL at every node in one line: A times I equals zero.

Common mistakes in topology. One: a tree that contains a loop, or one that misses a node. Two: counting the wrong number of nodes: a whole wire is one node. Three: forming a tie set with more than one link. Four: a cut set that does not split the graph into exactly two parts. Five: choosing a tree is free, many trees are possible, but the counts n minus one and b minus n plus one never change.
scenes.title: Common mistakes

parts.label: A whole wire is one node
Cut-set splits into exactly two parts

scenes.narration: Topology is how circuit simulators like SPICE work: they build the incidence matrix from your schematic and solve the equations automatically. Power system engineers use it to analyse grids with thousands of buses. Chip designers use it to check connections in millions of wires. And the same graph ideas appear in computer networks, road maps and social networks.
scenes.title: Topology at work

scenes.narration: Let's bring it together. A graph keeps only nodes and branches. A tree connects all nodes without loops, with n minus one twigs, and the rest are b minus n plus one links. Each link gives a tie set for KVL, each twig gives a cut set for KCL. And the incidence matrix lets a computer write KCL for the whole network at once.
scenes.title: Topology in one picture

scenes.narration: Sometimes we don't care about the inside of a network at all, only how it behaves between an input pair of terminals and an output pair, like an amplifier or a filter. Such a network is called a two port network, described by just four parameters. It is our next part.
